```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = FALSE
)
# Only the tiny example at the end of "How to use it" runs when the vignette
# is built (with 2 workers, the limit on CRAN). The timings are precomputed
# with tools/vignettes/parallel_results.R.
has_par <- requireNamespace("future.apply", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("parallelly", quietly = TRUE)
```

`find.design()` runs your simulation function many times, usually thousands of
times. By default these simulations run one after the other on a single CPU
core. Most computers have several cores, and with `parallel = TRUE` the
simulations are spread over them.

## When does it help?

It helps when a single call of your simulation function takes a noticeable
time, roughly 10 milliseconds or more. This is typical for simulation functions
that fit a model, for example a mixed model with `lme4::lmer()` or
`lme4::glmer()`, or an IRT model with `mirt::mirt()`. Then almost all of the
search time is spent in the simulations, and the search gets several times
faster.

For very fast simulation functions, such as a t-test, starting the workers and
sending them work costs more time than it saves. Keep the default
(`parallel = FALSE`) there.

You can time one call of your function to decide:

```{r}
system.time(for (i in 1:20) simfun(100))["elapsed"] / 20  # seconds per call
```

## How to use it

Install three helper packages once:

```{r}
install.packages(c("future", "future.apply", "parallelly"))
```

Then add `parallel = TRUE` to your call:

```{r}
library(mlpwr)
simfun <- example.simfun("multi1")  # a generalized linear mixed model (lme4::glmer)

set.seed(1)
ds <- find.design(simfun = simfun, boundaries = c(20, 200), power = .8,
                  evaluations = 1000, parallel = TRUE)
#> Running simulations on 7 parallel workers
summary(ds)
```

That is all. `parallel = TRUE` uses all CPU cores but one, so your computer
stays responsive. To choose the number yourself, give a number, e.g.
`parallel = 4`.

A tiny search on 2 cores (it is too small to be faster, it only shows the
mechanics):

```{r, eval = has_par}
library(mlpwr)
set.seed(1)
ds_small <- find.design(simfun = example.simfun("ttest"), boundaries = c(20, 200),
                        power = .8, evaluations = 200, parallel = 2, silent = TRUE)
ds_small$final$design
ds_small$settings$parallel
```

You don't need to do anything else: objects and packages that your simulation
function uses (for example a data set or `lme4`) are sent to the workers
automatically. It works the same way on Windows, macOS and Linux; the workers
are R sessions that run in the background and are closed when the search ends.

Only the simulations run in parallel. Fitting the surrogate model and choosing
the next designs happen in your R session as before, and the progress display
is the same.

## How much faster?

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Precomputed results (see tools/vignettes/parallel_results.R); if they are not
# available, a small comparison is run on 2 cores (nothing is written).
file_path <- system.file("extdata", "parallel_Vignette_results.RData",
                         package = "mlpwr")
if (nzchar(file_path)) {
  load(file_path)
} else if (has_par) {
  bench <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(FALSE, 2), function(p) {
    set.seed(1)
    t <- system.time(ds <- suppressWarnings(mlpwr::find.design(mlpwr::example.simfun("ttest"),
      boundaries = c(20, 200), power = .8, evaluations = 200, silent = TRUE,
      parallel = p)))[["elapsed"]]
    data.frame(workload = "ttest", simfun = "t-test (example.simfun(\"ttest\"))",
      ms_per_eval = NA, evaluations = ds$evaluations_used,
      parallel = if (isFALSE(p)) "FALSE" else "2", seconds = round(t, 1),
      design = ds$final$design[[1]], power = round(ds$final$power, 4))
  }))
  attr(bench, "machine") <- "the machine that built this vignette"
} else {
  bench <- NULL
}
tab <- function(wl) {
  b <- bench[bench$workload == wl, ]
  seq_time <- b$seconds[b$parallel == "FALSE"]
  data.frame(parallel = ifelse(b$parallel == "FALSE", "FALSE (sequential)",
                               ifelse(b$parallel == "1", "1 (sequential)", b$parallel)),
             seconds = b$seconds, speedup = ifelse(seq_time / b$seconds < .05, "< 0.1x",
                              paste0(round(seq_time / b$seconds, 1), "x")),
             design = b$design)
}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = "asis"}
if (!is.null(bench)) {
  cat("The tables show the time of the same search (seed 1) with different numbers of ",
      "cores, on ", attr(bench, "machine"), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  for (wl in unique(bench$workload)) {
    b <- bench[bench$workload == wl, ]
    cat("**", b$simfun[1], "**, ", b$evaluations[1], " evaluations",
        if (!is.na(b$ms_per_eval[1])) if (b$ms_per_eval[1] < 1) ", less than 1 ms per simulation" else
        paste0(", about ", round(b$ms_per_eval[1]), " ms per simulation"), ":\n\n", sep = "")
    print(knitr::kable(tab(wl), align = "lrrr"))
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  slow <- intersect(c("multi1", "irt1"), bench$workload)
  if (length(slow) > 0) {
    cat("For the slow simulation functions (",
        paste(c(multi1 = "glmer", irt1 = "mirt")[slow], collapse = ", "),
        ") the search gets faster with more cores. ", sep = "")
  }
  if ("ttest" %in% bench$workload) {
    cat("For the t-test, each simulation takes only a few milliseconds or ",
        "less, and sending the work to the workers costs more than it saves. ",
        sep = "")
  }
  cat("How much you gain depends on your computer and on how busy it is ",
      "(other computations running at the same time share the cores).\n\n",
      sep = "")
  cat("Note also the **design** column: all parallel runs (2 or more cores) ",
      "found exactly the same design, whatever the number of cores. The ",
      "sequential runs (`parallel = FALSE` or `1`) can find a slightly ",
      "different one, because they use different random numbers ",
      "(see the next section).\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Timings are not shown here, because the packages future.apply and ",
      "parallelly were not installed when this vignette was built.\n", sep = "")
}
```

## Reproducibility

With the same `set.seed()` a parallel search gives the same result every time,
and the result does not depend on the number of cores: `parallel = 2` and
`parallel = 8` find the same design. This is because every single simulation
gets its own stream of random numbers (L'Ecuyer-CMRG streams), no matter which
core runs it.

The random numbers are not the same as in a search with `parallel = FALSE`,
though, so a parallel search will not reproduce the exact numbers of a
sequential search with the same seed. Both are equally valid; they are just
different random draws. To reproduce a result, use the same seed and again a
sequential (`parallel = FALSE` or `1`) or a parallel search (any number of
cores from 2 up).

The setting is stored in the result, and `find.design(continue = ds)` keeps
using it unless you give `parallel` again.

## Things to know

* A simulation function runs in a separate R session, so changes it makes
  outside itself (for example a counter updated with `<<-`) are lost.
* If your simulation function fails, the error message names the design at
  which it failed.
* Printed output, messages and warnings of the simulation function are
  suppressed, as in the sequential mode.

## Advanced: your own future plan

The workers are managed by the [future](https://future.futureverse.org/)
package. If you want the simulations to run somewhere else, for example on
several machines, set a plan before the search and use `parallel = TRUE`:

```{r}
future::plan(future::cluster, workers = c("machine1", "machine2"))
ds <- find.design(simfun = simfun, boundaries = c(20, 200), power = .8,
                  parallel = TRUE)
#> Running simulations on 2 parallel workers (using your future::plan())
```

A plan that you set yourself (any plan other than the default sequential one)
is used as it is when `parallel = TRUE`. mlpwr has to be installed on all
workers. With a number, e.g. `parallel = 4`, `find.design()` starts its own
local workers for this call and switches back to your plan afterwards.
